# Self-Evolve With a Reference: Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents

Wenjie Liao Affiliation: Waseda University  
jie3040@akane.waseda.jp    Liangjie Zhao Affiliation: Adelaide
University  
zhaoliangjie55@gmail.com, Jimmy.Cao@adelaide.edu.au    Zehong Cao
Affiliation: Adelaide University  
zhaoliangjie55@gmail.com, Jimmy.Cao@adelaide.edu.au

7 October 2026

###### Abstract

Self-evolving tool-integrated agents learn from tasks and feedback
generated within their own training loop. A Curriculum Agent generates
tasks, while an Executor Agent learns from self-consistency signals
through reinforcement learning. However, relying solely on the current
Executor for feedback has two limitations: group-relative advantages
vanish under full consensus, while uncertainty-based curriculum rewards
favor disagreement without showing whether the generated tasks support
further learning. These limitations motivate an additional reference
beyond the current Executor. We propose AnchorLoop, which introduces a
frozen copy of the previous iteration’s Executor as a historical
reference and reuses it on both sides of the training loop. For the
Executor, the anchor provides a cross-reference advantage that evaluates
current outputs against both current and historical majority answers.
For the Curriculum, it provides an agreement-based reference based on
differences in sampled majority agreement. Since the Executor and anchor
have identical parameters during Curriculum training, this comparison
serves as a proxy for task selection rather than evidence of
inter-version improvement or correctness. Across 13 reasoning
benchmarks, AnchorLoop improves over Agent0 by 2.5% on mathematical
reasoning and 2.8% on general reasoning tasks. It also maintains higher
effective-advantage variance and continues improving in later iterations
as the unanchored baseline shows diminishing gains. These results
demonstrate the benefit of introducing a lightweight historical
reference into self-evolving tool-integrated agents without external
task or answer supervision.

###### keywords

Tool-Integrated Agents, Reference, Reinforcement Learning

## 1 Introduction

Tool-integrated language model agents can learn to solve complex tasks
through multi-turn interaction with external tools. Recent work further
extends this capability toward _self-evolution_, where agents generate
not only solutions but also their own training tasks and feedback. A
representative paradigm couples a Curriculum Agent that generates tasks
with an Executor Agent that learns to solve them through reinforcement
learning \[[25](#bib.bib6)\]. By generating tasks and feedback within
the training loop, such systems reduce their reliance on externally
supplied training tasks and answer labels. This creates a closed
learning loop in which the Executor serves not only as the learner, but
also as a source of feedback for training both agents.

This reliance on the current Executor, however, creates limitations on
both sides of self-evolution. On the Executor side, group-relative
learning relies on differences among sampled outputs. When all outputs
in a group reach consensus, the centered advantages vanish and provide
no relative preference among trajectories. On the Curriculum side,
uncertainty can identify tasks that elicit disagreement from the
Executor, but disagreement alone does not indicate whether those tasks
provide useful opportunities for further learning. In both cases, the
learning signal is determined entirely by the current Executor, without
a reference beyond its present behavior.

These limitations motivate a natural question: _can self-evolution gain
an additional reference while remaining self-contained?_ Our key idea is
to use the system’s own recent history as that reference. Specifically,
we retain the Executor from the previous iteration as a frozen _anchor_.
This introduces a temporal comparison without requiring externally
supplied tasks or answer labels. Historical reference models have been
used in iterative learning; for example, SPIN compares against responses
from a previous model while retaining human reference responses
\[[2](#bib.bib3)\]. Our focus is different: we study how a recent
Executor can serve as a shared reference for both sides of a
self-evolving Curriculum–Executor loop.

Based on this idea, we propose AnchorLoop, which reuses the same
historical anchor on both sides of self-evolution. For the Executor, the
anchor provides a _cross-reference advantage_ that evaluates current
outputs against both the current and anchor majority answers, augmenting
the preference induced by current self-consistency. For the Curriculum,
the anchor provides an agreement-based reference through the positive
difference in sampled majority-agreement rates. The anchor is refreshed
from the previous Executor at the beginning of each outer iteration and
remains frozen throughout that iteration.

Importantly, the two uses of the anchor have different interpretations.
Curriculum training precedes Executor training in each iteration, so the
current Executor and the newly refreshed anchor have identical
parameters during the Curriculum stage and produce independent rollout
groups. Their sampled agreement difference therefore serves as an
agreement-based proxy for shaping the Curriculum reward, rather than
direct evidence of improvement between model versions or correctness.
During subsequent Executor training, the current Executor evolves while
the anchor remains fixed, enabling a genuine historical comparison. We
further characterize this historical advantage and show that it acts as
a conditional reweighting of current outputs: it can introduce
additional relative information when current and historical majorities
differ, while still vanishing under full current consensus.

Our contributions are threefold:

- •
  Historical Anchoring. We introduce AnchorLoop, which uses the previous
  iteration’s Executor as a shared historical reference for both
  Curriculum and Executor training.
- •
  Dual-Sided Learning. We develop a cross-reference advantage for
  Executor training and an agreement-based reference for Curriculum
  training, and characterize how the historical reference shapes both
  learning signals.
- •
  Empirical Validation. Across two backbones and thirteen reasoning
  benchmarks, AnchorLoop consistently improves over the unanchored
  baseline by 2.5-2.8% points on average, while continuing to improve in
  later training iterations.

## 2 Preliminaries

Self-Evolving Curriculum–Executor Learning. We consider a self-evolving
system consisting of a Curriculum Agent $`\pi_{\theta}`$ and an Executor
Agent $`\pi_{\phi}`$. The Curriculum generates training tasks $`x`$,
while the Executor learns to solve them through multi-turn interaction
with external tools. Given a task $`x`$, the Executor generates a
trajectory $`\tau=(s_{1},a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,s_{H},a_{H},o_{H})`$ of at
most $`H`$ turns, where $`a_{h}`$ is either a tool call or a final
answer and $`o_{h}`$ is the resulting observation. The trajectory
terminates when the Executor produces a final answer
$`o(\tau)\in\mathcal{Y}`$ or reaches the turn budget \[[26](#bib.bib2),
[25](#bib.bib6)\]. The Curriculum–Executor loop generates both training
tasks and learning signals within the training process. The Curriculum
evaluates generated tasks based on the current Executor’s behavior,
while the Executor learns from agreement among its own sampled outputs.
Thus, both sides of self-evolution rely on feedback derived from the
current Executor \[[25](#bib.bib6)\].

Agreement-Based Group-Relative Learning. For each task $`x`$, the
Executor samples $`G`$ trajectories $`\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$. A fixed
final-answer parser maps each well-formed output to a canonical answer
$`o_{i}`$. Following self-consistency \[[23](#bib.bib9)\], the unique
modal answer among valid outputs defines a pseudo-label $`\tilde{y}`$,
and each trajectory receives

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       r_{i}=\mathbb{I}[o_{i}=\tilde{y}].
       ```                                 |     | (1) |

Invalid or missing outputs receive zero reward and do not vote for
$`\tilde{y}`$, while groups without a unique modal answer are unresolved
and excluded from updates that require a pseudo-label.

The reward $`r_{i}`$ measures _agreement_ rather than independently
verified _correctness_: the pseudo-label $`\tilde{y}`$ is determined
entirely by the sampled outputs. A consistent but incorrect group can
therefore receive the same agreement reward as a consistent correct
group.

Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) \[[20](#bib.bib1)\] normalizes
these rewards within the sampled group:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\mu}{\sigma+\varepsilon},
       ```                                          |     | (2) |

where $`\mu`$ and $`\sigma`$ denote the mean and standard deviation of
the group rewards, and $`\varepsilon>0`$ is a stabilizer. The policy is
then optimized using a clipped surrogate objective in the style of PPO
\[[19](#bib.bib12)\]. When all trajectories agree on the same valid
answer, $`r_{i}=1`$ for all $`i`$, yielding $`A_{i}=0`$. Thus, the
centered group-relative advantage provides no relative preference within
a fully consensual group.

![Refer to caption](2610.09856v1/figure_1.png)

Figure 1: Overview of AnchorLoop. The left panel illustrates an
unanchored two-agent self-evolution loop that can plateau. At outer
iteration $`t`$, AnchorLoop copies the previous Executor into a frozen
anchor and reuses it on both sides of the loop. During Curriculum
training, the current Executor and anchor have identical parameters but
produce independent rollout groups for the agreement-based reference
reward. All format-valid tasks form the same-iteration task pool
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. During Executor training, the anchor remains fixed
while the current Executor is updated. Current groups are resampled at
every inner step, whereas one anchor group per task and Curriculum batch
is cached and reused to construct the cross-reference advantage.

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Historical Anchor for Self-Evolution

AnchorLoop introduces a historical reference into the
Curriculum–Executor loop defined in Section
[2](#S2 "2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
At outer iteration $`t`$, we retain the previous iteration’s Executor as
a frozen anchor,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \pi^{\mathrm{anc}}\leftarrow\pi_{\phi}^{(t-1)},
       ```                                              |     | (3) |

and hold it fixed throughout the iteration. The anchor therefore
represents the most recently completed Executor while requiring no
externally supplied tasks or answer labels.

The same anchor is reused on both sides of self-evolution, but with
different roles. For Executor training, it provides a historical
majority answer used to construct a cross-reference advantage (Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Executor: Cross-Reference Advantage ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")).
For Curriculum training, it provides an additional rollout group whose
sampled agreement is compared with that of the current Executor (Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Curriculum: Anchor-Referenced Reward ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")).
The anchor is refreshed at the beginning of every outer iteration, as
illustrated in Figure
[1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
Figure
[1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
is schematic, and Equation
([11](#S3.E11 "In Complete Curriculum reward. ‣ 3.3 Curriculum: Anchor-Referenced Reward ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"))
defines the complete Curriculum reward.

The Curriculum and Executor are initialized from the same base model
$`\pi_{\mathrm{base}}`$ and updated separately. The Curriculum is
optimized with GRPO \[[20](#bib.bib1)\], while the Executor uses ADPO
\[[25](#bib.bib6)\]. Curriculum training precedes Executor training
within each outer iteration. This update order gives the anchor
different interpretations across the two stages, as detailed in Section
[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Alternating Training with an Iterative Anchor ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").

### 3.2 Executor: Cross-Reference Advantage

The current agreement reward provides a relative preference only when
answers within a group differ. AnchorLoop augments this current-only
signal with an anchor-based comparison that changes how current outputs
are weighted. Because the anchor remains fixed throughout the iteration,
it provides a common historical reference as the Executor updates. This
design does not guarantee a nonzero advantage for every task or prevent
all forms of training stagnation.

##### Current and anchor references.

For each task $`x`$ in the Executor stage, we sample $`G`$ trajectories
from the current Executor and another $`G`$ trajectories from the
anchor. Each resolved group follows the definition in Section
[2](#S2 "2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
to produce a pseudo-label, $`\tilde{y}^{\mathrm{cur}}`$ for the current
group and $`\tilde{y}^{\mathrm{anc}}`$ for the anchor group. If either
group is unresolved, the task is omitted from the pseudo-label-dependent
Executor update. Anchor rollouts are cached at the granularity of a
Curriculum batch and reused across the inner Executor steps that use the
same tasks, amortizing anchor sampling across those steps.

Let $`o_{i}`$ denote the parsed valid answer of current Executor
trajectory $`i`$. Invalid and missing trajectories receive zero for both
indicators. Each current trajectory receives two outcomes,

|     |                                        |                                                               |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle r_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{I}[o_{i}=\tilde{y}^{\mathrm{cur}}],`$ |     | (4) |
|     | $`\displaystyle r_{i}^{\mathrm{anc}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{I}[o_{i}=\tilde{y}^{\mathrm{anc}}].`$ |     |     |

Both indicators score the same current answer $`o_{i}`$. The first
measures agreement with the current group’s majority, whereas the second
measures agreement with the anchor group’s majority rather than scoring
an anchor trajectory.

##### Cross-reference advantage.

We form two advantages by centering and normalizing over the current
group:

|     |                                         |                                                                                                            |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle A_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}}`$  | $`\displaystyle=\frac{r_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}}-\mu^{\mathrm{cur}}}{\sigma^{\mathrm{cur}}+\varepsilon},`$       |     | (5) |
|     | $`\displaystyle A_{i}^{\mathrm{hist}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{(r_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}}-r_{i}^{\mathrm{anc}})-\bar{\Delta}}{s^{\Delta}+\varepsilon},`$ |     |     |

where $`\mu^{\mathrm{cur}}`$ and $`\sigma^{\mathrm{cur}}`$ are the mean
and standard deviation of $`r^{\mathrm{cur}}`$, while $`\bar{\Delta}`$
and $`s^{\Delta}`$ are the mean and standard deviation of
$`r^{\mathrm{cur}}-r^{\mathrm{anc}}`$. The cross-reference advantage
combines the two:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\hat{A}_{i}=(1-\alpha)A_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}}+\alpha A_{i}^{\mathrm{hist}},\qquad 0\leq\alpha\leq 1,
``` |  | (6) |

where $`\alpha`$ controls the contribution of the historical advantage.

##### Properties of the historical term.

The historical term acts as a conditional reweighting of current
outputs. For resolved current and anchor groups with $`\varepsilon>0`$,
several boundary cases clarify its behavior. If the two majority labels
agree, the two indicators coincide and $`A_{i}^{\mathrm{hist}}=0`$. If
all current answers are identical,
$`r_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}}-r_{i}^{\mathrm{anc}}`$ is constant across the
current group even when the majority labels differ. Centering therefore
makes both advantage terms zero. A different anchor label alone cannot
restore a relative preference within a fully consensual current group.

When the two majority labels differ and the current group contains only
those two answers, with both present, the historical advantage is a
positive rescaling of the current advantage. If the anchor’s majority
answer is absent from the current group, the two advantages are
identical. With additional answer classes, the historical term can
distinguish outputs that match the anchor majority from other outputs
that disagree with the current majority. Its contribution therefore
depends on the sampled answer composition. These group-level relations
do not establish equivalence between complete training runs.

Refreshing the anchor ties its parameters to the most recently completed
Executor iteration. This does not establish that the anchor remains
informative on every task, nor that a reference fixed to the base model
must necessarily become uninformative.

### 3.3 Curriculum: Anchor-Referenced Reward

The Curriculum evaluates each generated task using sampled behavior from
the current Executor. AnchorLoop augments this current-only signal with
an independently sampled rollout group from the anchor. We first define
the inherited task-level Curriculum terms and then introduce the
anchor-referenced component.

##### Base Curriculum reward.

Each candidate task $`x`$ is evaluated with $`G`$ current Executor
trajectories $`\{\tau_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}`$. Let $`n_{y}(x)`$ denote the
number of valid parsed answers with canonical label $`y`$. We define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\max}(x)=\frac{1}{G}\max_{y}n_{y}(x),\qquad R_{\mathrm{unc}}(x)=1-2\left|p_{\max}(x)-\frac{1}{2}\right|.
``` |  | (7) |

If no trajectory has a valid answer, we set $`p_{\max}(x)=0`$. The
maximum count remains defined when several labels tie, although such a
group has no pseudo-label. Invalid and missing trajectories do not add
to any label count and remain in the fixed denominator $`G`$.

Let $`N_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau_{j})`$ denote the number of Python calls
executed by the sandbox before trajectory $`j`$ terminates. Calls
executed before an invalid or missing final answer are still counted.
With call cap $`C`$, the task-level tool-use term is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{\mathrm{tool}}(x)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\min\!\left(N_{\mathrm{tool}}(\tau_{j}),C\right).
``` |  | (8) |

For a Curriculum batch $`\mathcal{B}`$ of $`B`$ candidate tasks, we
compute pairwise BLEU distances between task texts and connect two tasks
when their distance is below $`d_{\mathrm{rep}}`$. Let
$`\mathcal{C}(x)`$ denote the connected component containing $`x`$. The
repetition term is

|     |                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R_{\mathrm{rep}}(x)=\frac{|\mathcal{C}(x)|}{B}.
       ```                                              |     | (9) |

The binary gate $`R_{\mathrm{fmt}}(x)`$ equals one when the generated
task passes the fixed Problem: and Answer: format in Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Curriculum Agent Prompt ‣ Appendix B Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"),
and zero otherwise.

##### Anchor-referenced agreement.

We augment these inherited terms with an anchor comparison. For each
candidate task $`x`$, we define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
R_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)=\max\!\bigl(0,\,\mu^{\mathrm{cur}}(x)-\mu^{\mathrm{anc}}(x)\bigr),
``` |  | (10) |

where $`\mu^{\mathrm{cur}}(x)`$ and $`\mu^{\mathrm{anc}}(x)`$ are the
majority agreement rates of the current Executor and anchor,
respectively. For a resolved group, each rate is the number of rollouts
matching its own unique modal answer divided by the fixed $`G`$. Invalid
and missing outputs contribute zero to the numerator but remain in the
denominator. If either group is unresolved, we set
$`R_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)=0`$; the uncertainty, tool-use, repetition, and
format terms remain defined.

Importantly, $`\mu^{\mathrm{anc}}(x)`$ is computed over anchor outputs
and is not the current-group mean of $`r_{i}^{\mathrm{anc}}`$ defined in
Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Executor: Cross-Reference Advantage ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
Moreover, the two agreement rates are computed with respect to their
respective group majorities rather than a shared ground-truth answer.

##### Interpretation.

The reference term measures a difference in sampled *agreement*, not a
difference in *correctness*. A positive $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)`$ means
that the sampled current group has a larger majority fraction than the
sampled anchor group. It does not establish that the current Executor is
more accurate, nor that it can solve a task that the anchor cannot. In
particular, a more concentrated but incorrect answer distribution can
also receive a positive score.

The update order imposes a second limitation on this interpretation.
Because Curriculum training precedes Executor training, the current
Executor and the newly refreshed anchor have identical parameters during
the Curriculum stage and differ only through independent sampling. Their
sampled agreement rates may therefore differ, but such a difference is
not evidence of progress between historical model versions. Taking the
positive part does not remove this sampling variation. We consequently
use $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ as an agreement-based proxy for Curriculum
shaping rather than as a measure of correctness or inter-version
improvement.

##### Complete Curriculum reward.

We combine the reference term with the inherited uncertainty, tool-use,
repetition, and format-validity terms:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle R_{C}(x)=R_{\mathrm{fmt}}(x)\max\!\big(`$ | $`\displaystyle 0,\,w_{\mathrm{unc}}R_{\mathrm{unc}}(x)+w_{\mathrm{tool}}R_{\mathrm{tool}}(x)`$ |  | (11) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-w_{\mathrm{rep}}R_{\mathrm{rep}}(x)+\lambda R_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\big).`$ |  |  |

The base reward weights used throughout the reported training runs are
listed in Table
[3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ ADPO configuration. ‣ A.2 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
When $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)=0`$, the remaining components of $`R_{C}(x)`$
remain active; a zero reference term therefore does not by itself
discard the task.

Input: Base model $`\pi_{\mathrm{base}}`$, outer iterations $`T`$

Initialize separate agents
$`\pi_{\theta},\pi_{\phi}\leftarrow\pi_{\mathrm{base}}`$

for *$`t=1,\dots,T`$* do

   Set $`\pi^{\mathrm{anc}}\leftarrow\pi_{\phi}^{(t-1)}`$ and freeze the
anchor for iteration $`t`$

   Keep $`\pi_{\phi}`$ fixed; update only $`\pi_{\theta}`$ via GRPO with
reward $`R_{C}`$; collect all format-valid tasks in $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$
while retaining their Curriculum batch assignments

   Keep $`\pi_{\theta}`$ fixed; update only $`\pi_{\phi}`$ on
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ via ADPO using the scaled cross-reference advantage
$`\widetilde{A}`$

   Resample each current group at every Executor inner step and reuse
one cached anchor group per task and Curriculum batch

   Discard $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ and its rollout cache, and denote the
resulting Executor by $`\pi_{\phi}^{(t)}`$

end for

Output: Trained Executor $`\pi_{\phi}^{(T)}`$

Algorithm 1 Training procedure of AnchorLoop.

### 3.4 Alternating Training with an Iterative Anchor

AnchorLoop alternates Curriculum and Executor training over $`T`$ outer
iterations. Let $`\pi_{\phi}^{(t)}`$ denote the Executor after iteration
$`t`$, with $`\pi_{\phi}^{(0)}=\pi_{\mathrm{base}}`$. At the beginning
of iteration $`t`$, we refresh the anchor as

|     |                                                |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \pi^{\mathrm{anc}}\leftarrow\pi_{\phi}^{(t-1)}
       ```                                             |     | (12) |

and keep it frozen throughout the iteration.

##### Curriculum stage.

We first fix the Executor and update only the Curriculum Agent using
GRPO with the reward $`R_{C}`$ from Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Curriculum: Anchor-Referenced Reward ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
The current Executor and newly refreshed anchor therefore have identical
parameters $`\pi_{\phi}^{(t-1)}`$ during this stage and differ only
through independent sampling.

All format-valid tasks generated during Curriculum training form the
same-iteration task pool $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$, with their Curriculum
batch assignments preserved. We do not filter these tasks according to
$`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ or the total Curriculum reward $`R_{C}`$. The
Curriculum-generated Answer: field is used only for format checking and
is neither provided to the Executor nor used as a supervision label.

##### Executor stage.

We then freeze the Curriculum Agent and update only the Executor on
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. The anchor remains fixed at $`\pi_{\phi}^{(t-1)}`$,
while the current Executor evolves during optimization, providing the
historical comparison used by the cross-reference advantage in Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Executor: Cross-Reference Advantage ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").

Each task remains fixed across the Executor inner steps associated with
its Curriculum batch. For each task, the current Executor resamples
$`G`$ trajectories at every inner step, whereas the anchor group is
sampled once per task and Curriculum batch and cached across the
corresponding Executor updates. Current groups are not retained between
inner steps. After the Executor stage, the resulting policy is denoted
$`\pi_{\phi}^{(t)}`$. The task pool $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$ and all cached
rollouts are then discarded. The next outer iteration generates a new
task pool and does not replay tasks from earlier iterations.

##### Policy optimization.

For Curriculum training, the Curriculum Agent’s group consists of a
batch of generated tasks. Each task is scored by $`R_{C}`$ from Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Curriculum: Anchor-Referenced Reward ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"),
and the resulting rewards are normalized across the task batch to form
the GRPO advantages.

For Executor training, each group consists of the $`G`$ trajectories
sampled for a single task. The standard group-relative advantage is
replaced by the cross-reference advantage $`\hat{A}_{i}`$ from Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Executor: Cross-Reference Advantage ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
The Executor follows ADPO \[[25](#bib.bib6)\], which scales the
advantage according to current answer agreement and dynamically adjusts
the upper clipping bound.

For each task $`x`$, we compute the current-group agreement score

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\hat{p}(x)=\mu^{\mathrm{cur}}(x)=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}r_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}},
``` |  | (13) |

where $`\hat{p}(x)`$ is the fraction of current outputs matching the
current group’s modal answer. Let $`s(x)=f(\hat{p}(x))`$ denote the ADPO
task weight, where $`f`$ is nondecreasing. We apply this weight to the
complete cross-reference advantage:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\widetilde{A}_{i}(x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=s(x)\hat{A}_{i}`$ |  | (14) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=s(x)\left[(1-\alpha)A_{i}^{\mathrm{cur}}+\alpha A_{i}^{\mathrm{hist}}\right].`$ |  |  |

Thus, the same task weight scales both the current and historical
components. The clipping interval is

|     |                                                              |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       [1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},\,1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}(x)],
       ```                                                           |     |

where $`\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}(x)=g(\hat{p}(x))`$ and $`g`$ is
nonincreasing. Thus, both the task weight and the upper clipping bound
are recomputed from the current group’s agreement score.

##### Token-level Executor objective.

Let $`y_{i,\ell}`$ denote the token generated at position $`\ell`$ of
trajectory $`i`$, and let $`h_{i,\ell}`$ contain the task, preceding
generated tokens, and any tool observations returned before that
position. Tool observations condition subsequent generation but are not
themselves optimized. We use a mask $`m_{i,\ell}`$ over generated
reasoning, tool-call, and final-answer tokens, with
$`M_{i}=\sum_{\ell}m_{i,\ell}`$.

The behavior policy $`\pi_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}}}`$ is frozen before
sampling the current group at each Executor inner step. The token-level
importance ratio is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{i,\ell}(\phi)=\frac{\pi_{\phi}(y_{i,\ell}\mid h_{i,\ell})}{\pi_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,\ell}\mid h_{i,\ell})}.
``` |  | (15) |

The same trajectory-level advantage $`\widetilde{A}_{i}(x)`$ is applied
to all optimized tokens in trajectory $`i`$. The Executor objective is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{exec}}(\phi)={}`$ | $`\displaystyle-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{M_{i}}\sum_{\ell}m_{i,\ell}\min\!\Bigl(\rho_{i,\ell}(\phi)\widetilde{A}_{i}(x),`$ |  | (16) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\rho_{i,\ell}(\phi),1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}(x)\right)\widetilde{A}_{i}(x)\Bigr)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\frac{\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{M_{i}}\sum_{\ell}m_{i,\ell}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid h_{i,\ell})\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid h_{i,\ell})\right),`$ |  |  |

where the KL reference is the frozen base model,
$`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{\mathrm{base}}`$.

The anchor adds one frozen Executor checkpoint to storage at any given
time. Its rollouts are cached at the task–Curriculum-batch level,
amortizing anchor sampling across the corresponding Executor inner
steps. Overall, the anchor serves as an independently sampled reference
during Curriculum training and becomes a historical reference as the
Executor subsequently updates. Algorithm
[1](#algorithm1 "In Complete Curriculum reward. ‣ 3.3 Curriculum: Anchor-Referenced Reward ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
summarizes the complete training procedure, while the corresponding
functions and hyperparameters are reported in Appendix
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
provides the Curriculum and Executor prompts, together with the
answer-parsing and group-resolution rules.

## 4 Experiments and Results

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

##### Training Details.

We evaluate AnchorLoop on two open-source base models, Qwen3-4B-Base
\[[27](#bib.bib13)\] and MiMo-7B-Base \[[11](#bib.bib21)\]. For each
backbone, the Curriculum Agent, Executor Agent, and initial anchor are
derived from the same base model. We implement AnchorLoop on VeRL
\[[21](#bib.bib20)\] with a sandboxed Python interpreter provided by
VeRL-Tool. A complete \<python\>–\</python\> block triggers one
subprocess call, whose standard output is returned to the model as the
next observation. Training follows the alternating procedure in Section
[3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Alternating Training with an Iterative Anchor ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
Each outer iteration consists of a Curriculum stage followed by an
Executor stage. All format-valid tasks generated during Curriculum
training enter the same-iteration Executor task pool $`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$
while retaining their Curriculum batch assignments; we apply neither
reward-based task filtering nor task replay across outer iterations. For
each task, the current Executor samples $`G=8`$ trajectories at every
Executor inner step, whereas the anchor samples $`G=8`$ trajectories
once per task and Curriculum batch and reuses them across the
corresponding inner steps. The anchor is refreshed from the previous
iteration’s Executor at the beginning of each outer iteration and
remains frozen throughout that iteration.

Unless otherwise specified, we report models after three outer
iterations. Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
uses this setting for both backbones, while the anchor-refresh analysis
in Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Contribution of the two anchor signals. ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(a)
additionally extends training to a fourth iteration. AnchorLoop uses no
externally supplied training tasks or answer labels during
self-evolution; the Curriculum Agent generates the complete Executor
training task pool. Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
provides the full training configuration, hyperparameters, and sandbox
settings.

##### Baselines and Benchmarks.

We compare against seven baselines: two no-training references (Base
Model and Base Model w/ Tool), four self-evolving methods (Absolute Zero
\[[28](#bib.bib5)\], SPIRAL \[[10](#bib.bib7)\], R-Zero
\[[6](#bib.bib4)\], and Socratic-Zero \[[22](#bib.bib8)\]), and Agent0
\[[25](#bib.bib6)\], the direct unanchored baseline underlying our
two-agent training setup.

We evaluate mathematical reasoning on seven benchmarks: AMC23
\[[17](#bib.bib27)\], MATH-500 \[[5](#bib.bib15), [9](#bib.bib11)\],
GSM8K \[[3](#bib.bib10)\], Minerva \[[8](#bib.bib14)\], OlympiadBench
\[[4](#bib.bib16)\], AIME24 \[[13](#bib.bib25), [14](#bib.bib26)\], and
AIME25 \[[15](#bib.bib28), [16](#bib.bib29)\]. General reasoning is
evaluated on six benchmarks: SuperGPQA \[[12](#bib.bib17)\], MMLU-Pro
\[[24](#bib.bib18)\], BBEH \[[7](#bib.bib19)\], GPQA-Diamond
\[[18](#bib.bib22)\], HumanEval \[[1](#bib.bib23)\], and AGIEval
\[[29](#bib.bib24)\]. We report greedy pass@1 except mean@32 for AMC23
\[[17](#bib.bib27)\] and AIME. Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Baselines and Benchmark Details ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
provides baseline adaptations, dataset details, and the complete
evaluation and aggregation protocol.

### 4.2 Main Results

Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
compares AnchorLoop with the seven baselines across thirteen reasoning
benchmarks. Overall, historical anchoring consistently improves over the
unanchored Agent0 baseline on both backbones and across both evaluation
domains.

##### Mathematical reasoning.

As shown in Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"),
AnchorLoop achieves a Math AVG of $`55.2`$ on Qwen3-4B-Base and $`63.5`$
on MiMo-7B-Base, improving over Agent0 by $`2.5`$ percentage points on
both backbones. Relative to the tool-augmented base models, the
corresponding gains are $`11.2`$ and $`7.0`$ points. The improvement is
also consistent at the benchmark level: AnchorLoop obtains the highest
reported score in every mathematical benchmark column on both backbones,
including AIME24 and AIME25.

##### General reasoning.

Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
shows a similar pattern outside the mathematical domain. AnchorLoop
reaches a General AVG of $`47.9`$ on Qwen3-4B-Base and $`42.8`$ on
MiMo-7B-Base, exceeding Agent0 by $`2.8`$ and $`2.7`$ percentage points,
respectively. It also obtains the highest reported score in every
general-reasoning benchmark column on both backbones. These improvements
are notable because the Curriculum generates mathematical training
tasks, whereas the evaluation spans knowledge-intensive reasoning,
coding, and general problem solving. The results therefore show that the
gains associated with historical anchoring are not confined to the
mathematical benchmarks used to characterize the training distribution.

Appendix Table
[4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ C.2 Evaluation Benchmarks ‣ Appendix C Baselines and Benchmark Details ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
reports the mean and sample standard deviation over five independent
training runs. These statistics characterize run-to-run variability
rather than statistical significance. Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
further reports per-benchmark trajectories, iteration dynamics, and
sensitivity results on MiMo-7B-Base.

### 4.3 Training Dynamics

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Training dynamics on Qwen3-4B-Base. (a) Math AVG across three
outer iterations. (b) Within-group variance of the effective Executor
advantage, $`V_{\mathrm{adv}}`$, averaged over sampled groups. By
iteration 3, it decreases to $`0.07`$ for Agent0 but remains at $`0.28`$
for AnchorLoop. (c) Fraction of Curriculum tasks with a positive sampled
reference gap. An unresolved current–reference pair contributes zero.
The fraction decreases from $`54.7\%`$ initially to $`16.1\%`$ for
Agent0 and $`32.9\%`$ for AnchorLoop by iteration 3.

##### Later-iteration performance.

Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(a)
tracks Math AVG across the three outer iterations. Agent0 improves by
$`5.8`$ points in the first iteration, but its incremental gains
decrease to $`2.0`$ and $`0.9`$ points in iterations 2 and 3. AnchorLoop
begins from the same initialization and shows a comparable early
improvement, while retaining gains of $`2.8`$ and $`2.0`$ points in the
subsequent iterations. Consequently, the gap between the two methods
grows across later training and reaches $`2.5`$ points after iteration
3. This pattern motivates examining whether the learning signals
available to the two methods evolve differently over training.

##### Effective advantage variance.

Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(b)
measures the within-group variance of the final effective Executor
advantage. Let $`\mathcal{B}_{t}`$ contain all sampled Executor groups
across the update steps of outer iteration $`t`$. For group size $`G`$
and final ADPO-scaled advantage $`\widetilde{A}_{b,i}`$, we compute

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V_{\mathrm{adv}}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_{t}|}\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}_{t}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\left(\widetilde{A}_{b,i}-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\widetilde{A}_{b,j}\right)^{2}\right].
``` |  |

Both methods begin at $`V_{\mathrm{adv}}=0.43`$. By iteration 3, Agent0
decreases to $`0.07`$, whereas AnchorLoop retains substantially more
within-group variation at $`0.28`$. This observation is consistent with
the motivation for cross-reference training: the anchored objective
preserves more differentiated effective advantages in the sampled groups
as training proceeds. It does not imply that the historical component is
nonzero for every group; as established in Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Executor: Cross-Reference Advantage ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"),
both components vanish when all current answers are identical. Nor does
this statistic alone establish that the increased variance causes the
performance improvement.

##### Positive reference-gap frequency.

Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(c)
examines the Curriculum side by reporting the fraction of generated
tasks for which the independently sampled current and reference groups
satisfy

|     |                                              |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mu^{\mathrm{cur}}(x)>\mu^{\mathrm{ref}}(x).
       ```                                           |     |

An unresolved group pair contributes zero and is not counted as
positive. For AnchorLoop, the reference group is sampled from the newly
refreshed anchor; for Agent0, we construct the diagnostic using a second
independent rollout group from the same Executor checkpoint. During
Curriculum training, the current and reference models have identical
parameters, and each agreement rate is computed against its own group’s
majority answer. The measured fraction decreases from $`54.7\%`$
initially to $`16.1\%`$ for Agent0 and $`32.9\%`$ for AnchorLoop by
iteration 3.

Consistent with the interpretation in Section
[3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Curriculum: Anchor-Referenced Reward ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"),
this statistic measures the frequency of positive sampled agreement
differences rather than correctness or inter-version progress. The
higher fraction observed for AnchorLoop therefore characterizes the
sampled Curriculum signal; it does not imply that the current Executor
has newly solved those tasks or establish that the reference reward
causes the subsequent performance difference.

### 4.4 Anchor Analysis

|                                               |          |             |
|-----------------------------------------------|----------|-------------|
| Method                                        | Math AVG | General AVG |
| Without tool access                           |          |             |
| Qwen3-4B (Base)                               | 42.6     | 37.2        |
| $`\hskip 9.24994pt+\,`$ SPIRAL                | 47.2     | 42.1        |
| $`\hskip 9.24994pt+\,`$ R-Zero                | 48.7     | 42.8        |
| With tool access                              |          |             |
| $`\hskip 9.24994pt+\,`$ TIR                   | 44.0     | 39.6        |
| $`\hskip 9.24994pt+\,`$ Absolute Zero         | 46.4     | 41.9        |
| Matched anchor variants with tool access      |          |             |
| Agent0                                        | 52.7     | 45.1        |
| $`\hskip 9.24994pt+\,R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ only  | 53.6     | 45.9        |

Table 2: Tool comparisons and anchor ablations on Qwen3-4B-Base. Agent0
and AnchorLoop are shared endpoints. Only the anchor variants use
matched training and evaluation settings.

##### Contribution of the two anchor signals.

The matched anchor block of Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
separates the two uses of the anchor: $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ on the
Curriculum side and $`A^{\mathrm{hist}}`$ on the Executor side. All four
configurations use the same Qwen3-4B-Base initialization, three outer
iterations, update steps, ADPO settings, tool environment, and
evaluation protocol. When the historical advantage is disabled, the
Executor uses $`A^{\mathrm{cur}}`$ with unit coefficient. When enabled,
it uses $`(1-\alpha)A^{\mathrm{cur}}+\alpha A^{\mathrm{hist}}`$ with
$`\alpha=0.6`$. Disabling the Curriculum reference sets $`\lambda=0`$
while leaving all other Curriculum rewards and task handling unchanged.

Adding $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ alone improves the Math and General averages
from $`52.7/45.1`$ to $`53.6/45.9`$, while adding $`A^{\mathrm{hist}}`$
alone reaches $`54.4/46.7`$. Combining both gives the full AnchorLoop
result of $`55.2/47.9`$. Thus, both anchor uses are associated with
improvements over the unanchored configuration in the matched setting,
with the Executor-side historical advantage producing the larger
individual change. The endpoint comparison does not, however, isolate
the mechanism behind either improvement or establish a synergistic
interaction between the two components.

![Refer to caption](2610.09856v1/figs/figure_3.png)

Figure 3: Anchor and Curriculum analyses on Qwen3-4B-Base. (a) Math AVG
across outer iterations with an iterative anchor versus an anchor fixed
to the base model. (b) Sensitivity over the historical-advantage weight
$`\alpha`$ and Curriculum reference weight $`\lambda`$ on a
$`4\times 4`$ grid; the default setting is
$`(\alpha,\lambda)=(0.6,0.4)`$. (c) Pass rate and average tool calls on
$`200`$ tasks sampled from each Curriculum stage. The iteration-1
Executor generates $`G=8`$ trajectories per task, and both statistics
are computed from the same $`1{,}600`$ trajectories per stage.

##### Iterative versus fixed anchor.

Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Contribution of the two anchor signals. ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(a)
tests whether refreshing the historical reference matters by comparing
AnchorLoop with an anchor permanently fixed to the base model. The two
settings remain close in the first iteration, but diverge as training
proceeds. The iterative and fixed variants reach $`55.2`$ and $`53.0`$
at iteration 3, respectively, and $`56.3`$ and $`53.3`$ at iteration 4.
These results show that refreshing the anchor with the most recently
completed Executor is associated with stronger later-iteration
performance in this setting. They do not establish that a fixed anchor
necessarily becomes uninformative, nor do they isolate checkpoint age as
the sole source of the difference.

##### Comparison across tool settings.

Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
places AnchorLoop alongside methods evaluated with and without tool
access under their respective training configurations. Adding the Python
tool to the untrained Qwen3-4B base model changes Math AVG from $`42.6`$
to $`44.0`$ and General AVG from $`37.2`$ to $`39.6`$. Among the
tool-integrated training methods, AnchorLoop reaches $`55.2/47.9`$,
compared with $`52.7/45.1`$ for Agent0.

These comparisons provide context for tool-integrated performance but
should not be interpreted as a controlled ablation of tool access. The
methods differ simultaneously in task generation, training objective,
and reward design. The comparisons across methods in Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
therefore do not isolate the causal contribution of either tool use or
historical anchoring. Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Anchor Mechanism Analysis ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
further analyzes the historical-advantage structure, computational cost,
anchor refresh and caching, and representative failure cases.

### 4.5 Curriculum Analysis

##### Sensitivity to $`\alpha`$ and $`\lambda`$.

Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Contribution of the two anchor signals. ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(b)
evaluates the two anchor-specific weights: the historical-advantage
weight $`\alpha`$, which balances $`A^{\mathrm{cur}}`$ and
$`A^{\mathrm{hist}}`$ in Executor training, and the Curriculum reference
weight $`\lambda`$, which scales $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$. Across the
$`4\times 4`$ grid, the default setting $`(\alpha,\lambda)=(0.6,0.4)`$
reaches a Math AVG of $`55.21`$, while all evaluated configurations
remain within $`1.5`$ points of this value. The result indicates limited
sensitivity within the evaluated range, although it does not
characterize settings outside the grid or remove the need to select the
two weights.

##### Evolution of Curriculum tasks and tool use.

We further examine how the generated task distribution changes across
Curriculum stages $`t=0,1,2,3`$. From each stage, we sample $`200`$
tasks and evaluate them using a fixed iteration-1 Executor, which
independently generates $`G=8`$ trajectories per task. We compute the
mean binary agreement reward and the average number of tool calls over
the same $`1{,}600`$ trajectories for each stage.

Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Contribution of the two anchor signals. ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(c)
shows that the measured pass rate under this fixed Executor decreases
from $`71.8\%`$ on $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Iter}\,0}`$ to $`39.4\%`$ on
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Iter}\,3}`$, while the average number of tool
calls per trajectory increases from $`1.32`$ to $`2.87`$. Because the
same Executor is used to evaluate tasks from all stages, these changes
indicate that the distribution of Curriculum-generated tasks evolves
over training: later task sets lower agreement reward and more tool
interactions from this fixed evaluator.

These statistics should not be interpreted as direct measures of task
difficulty or correctness. In particular, $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ compares
independently sampled agreement rates during Curriculum training rather
than identifying tasks that the current Executor can solve but the
anchor cannot. The observed trends therefore characterize how the
generated task and response distributions change alongside anchored
self-evolution; they do not by themselves establish that later tasks are
intrinsically harder, that additional tool calls are necessary, or that
$`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ causally produces either trend. Appendix
[F](#A6 "Appendix F Case Studies and Qualitative Examples ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
provides selected Curriculum tasks, post-update Executor comparisons,
and full reasoning traces.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduce AnchorLoop to address weakening feedback in self-evolving
Curriculum and Executor training. At each outer iteration, a frozen copy
of the previous Executor provides an independently sampled agreement
reference for Curriculum training and helps construct a cross-reference
advantage for Executor training, without external tasks or answer
labels. Across two backbones and thirteen benchmarks, AnchorLoop
improves Math AVG over Agent0 by 2.5 points and General AVG by 2.7 to
2.8 points. It also retains higher effective-advantage variance and
shows stronger gains in later iterations.

## Appendix A Experimental Details

### A.1 Training Setup

We implement AnchorLoop on top of VeRL \[[21](#bib.bib20)\] with the
VeRL-Tool extension providing a sandboxed Python interpreter that
executes each code block emitted by the Executor in a separate
subprocess. All experiments use 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. For AnchorLoop,
one outer iteration takes about 24 hours on Qwen3-4B-Base
\[[27](#bib.bib13)\] and about 36 hours on MiMo-7B-Base
\[[11](#bib.bib21)\]. Multiplying these per-iteration values gives
approximate three-iteration references of 72 and 108 hours. These
figures are estimates rather than separately measured total times.
Within each outer iteration, all tasks that pass the fixed Curriculum
output format are retained with their original batch assignments and
passed to the Executor stage. We do not select tasks by
$`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$, the total reward $`R_{C}`$, or a top-$`k`$ rule.
The Executor prompt contains the problem statement and any required
context. The Curriculum-generated Answer: field is used only to check
the generation format and is not shown to the Executor or used as a
training label.

A task remains fixed across the Executor inner steps assigned to its
Curriculum batch. The current Executor resamples $`G=8`$ trajectories at
every inner step. The anchor samples $`G=8`$ trajectories once per task
and batch, then reuses them across those steps. This amortizes anchor
sampling while keeping current rollouts aligned with the changing
Executor. The task pool, current groups, and anchor cache are discarded
after the Executor stage. The next outer iteration uses newly generated
tasks without replaying earlier tasks.

### A.2 Hyperparameters

Table
[3](#A1.T3 "Table 3 ‣ ADPO configuration. ‣ A.2 Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
summarizes the confirmed settings for both backbones. AnchorLoop use
ADPO functions and clipping configuration on Qwen3-4B-Base and
MiMo-7B-Base. The learning rate is lower for the larger MiMo backbone.
The weight $`\alpha=0.6`$ on the historical advantage and the weight
$`\lambda=0.4`$ on the reference reward are the defaults selected by the
sweeps.

##### Curriculum reward configuration.

The Executor group size is $`G=8`$, and the Curriculum batch size is
$`B=64`$. The tool-use term caps each trajectory at $`C=4`$ executed
calls. The repetition graph uses BLEU distance threshold
$`d_{\mathrm{rep}}=0.6`$. The format gate and nonnegative truncation
apply to the complete weighted sum. AnchorLoop use
$`w_{\mathrm{unc}}=1.0`$, $`w_{\mathrm{tool}}=0.25`$, and
$`w_{\mathrm{rep}}=0.20`$ on both backbones. These weights remain fixed
across all outer iterations.

##### ADPO configuration.

AnchorLoop configuration follows the functional form of Agent0’s
released ADPO implementation \[[25](#bib.bib6)\]. For an agreement score
$`p`$, let $`p_{\min}`$ and $`p_{\max}`$ delimit the interpolation
interval. We first map $`p`$ to a value in $`[0,1]`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q(p)=\min\!\left\{1,\max\!\left\{0,\frac{p-p_{\min}}{p_{\max}-p_{\min}}\right\}\right\}.
``` |  | (17) |

Let $`s_{\min}`$ be the minimum advantage weight, $`\epsilon_{0}`$ the
base clipping width, and $`\delta_{\epsilon}`$ the maximum increment to
the upper width. The functions in Section
[3](#S3 "3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
are instantiated as

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle f(p)`$ | $`\displaystyle=s_{\min}+(1-s_{\min})q(p),`$ |  | (18) |
|  | $`\displaystyle g(p)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\epsilon_{0}+\delta_{\epsilon}[1-q(p)],`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\epsilon_{0}.`$ |  |  |

With the listed values, $`f(p)`$ ranges from $`0.6`$ to $`1.0`$, and
$`g(p)`$ ranges from $`0.3`$ at low agreement to $`0.2`$ at high
agreement. The Executor’s clipping interval is therefore
$`[0.8,1+g(p)]`$. These functions saturate outside the interpolation
interval and do not by themselves filter tasks. The score $`p`$ is
recomputed from each current Executor group, and $`f(p)`$ scales the
complete mixed advantage. No additional normalization is applied to this
task weight.

The base width $`\epsilon_{0}=0.2`$ is also the Executor’s lower
clipping width, and the Curriculum uses the fixed width
$`\epsilon_{C}=0.2`$. Its clipping interval is
$`[1-\epsilon_{C},1+\epsilon_{C}]`$. At each Executor inner step, the
rollout policy is frozen as $`\pi_{\phi_{\mathrm{old}}}`$ before the
current group is sampled. Token-level PPO ratios use this behavior
policy. The KL term instead uses the frozen base model
$`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{\mathrm{base}}`$ on both backbones.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|

| Outer loop | Outer iterations $`T`$ | 3 |
|  | Group size $`G`$ | 8 |
|  | Curriculum inner steps $`K_{C}`$ | 32 |
|  | Executor inner steps $`K_{E}`$ | 128 |
| Anchor side | Historical advantage weight $`\alpha`$ | 0.6 |

|  | Learning rate (MiMo-7B) | $`5\times 10^{-7}`$ |
|  | KL coefficient $`\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}`$ | 0.01 |
|  | KL reference $`\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ | Frozen base model |
| Curriculum | Clip width $`\epsilon_{C}`$ | 0.2 |

### A.3 Sandbox Configuration

The Python interpreter runs in a stateless subprocess with an execution
timeout of 30 seconds and a memory limit of 1 GB per call. The standard
scientific stack is preinstalled, including NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, and the
standard math, fractions, and itertools modules. A tool call must be
enclosed by one complete \<python\> and \</python\> tag pair. Each
complete pair triggers one sandbox call. An incomplete or malformed pair
does not trigger execution. The interpreter’s standard output is
returned to the Executor as the next observation. The tool-use analysis
reports the configurations and evaluation settings shown in the main
paper. It does not provide a matched same-checkpoint comparison with the
Python tool disabled.

## Appendix B Prompt Templates

We present the prompt templates used by the Curriculum Agent and the
Executor Agent. Both prompts are kept short and remain unchanged
throughout the three outer iterations. The iterative anchor shapes the
policy distribution through the reward and the advantage, not through
prompt edits.

### B.1 Curriculum Agent Prompt

The Curriculum Agent generates one math problem per call. The prompt
asks for a self-contained problem with a single numerical answer that
the Executor can attempt through the tool interface defined above.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.2 Executor Agent Prompt

The Executor Agent receives the problem statement and produces a
trajectory that interleaves reasoning with Python tool calls. The prompt
instructs the Executor to wrap each code block in one complete
\<python\> and \</python\> pair. It also requires a final answer in a
fixed format that the consensus rule and binary reward can parse.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### B.3 Answer Parsing and Group Resolution

We parse the fixed final-answer field before comparing sampled outputs.
A well-formed output is mapped to one canonical answer label. An output
is invalid when the trajectory finishes but the field is absent,
malformed, or contains conflicting answers. A trajectory is missing when
it reaches a length limit, times out, terminates with an execution
failure, or returns empty output before a final answer. Invalid and
missing outputs do not vote for a modal label and receive reward zero,
but they remain in the fixed group size $`G=8`$.

A group is resolved only when its valid answers contain one label with a
unique highest count. A highest-count tie or the absence of a valid
answer makes the group unresolved. Such a group is omitted from an
Executor update that requires a pseudo-label. In a diagnostic average
over a fixed sampled pool, its pseudo-label-dependent contribution is
zero, so the stated denominator does not change. If either group in the
Curriculum comparison is unresolved, its frontier term is set to zero
while the uncertainty, tool-use, and repetition terms remain active. The
same parsing and resolution rules are used for current, anchor, and
reference groups.

## Appendix C Baselines and Benchmark Details

### C.1 Baseline Methods

We compare AnchorLoop against seven baselines that cover both untrained
references and published self-evolving training methods.

Base Model. The pre-trained Qwen3-4B-Base or MiMo-7B-Base backbone
evaluated without any further training and without access to the Python
interpreter.

Base Model w/ Tool (TIR). The same backbone with access to the Python
interpreter at inference time but no additional training.

Absolute Zero \[[28](#bib.bib5)\]. A zero-data framework in which the
model proposes code reasoning tasks and solves them through Python
execution. It is trained without external tasks or labels. In our
adaptation, the Python interpreter is available during both training and
evaluation.

SPIRAL \[[10](#bib.bib7)\]. A self-play reinforcement learning method
that trains a shared policy through multi-turn self-play in TextArena
zero-sum games.

R-Zero \[[6](#bib.bib4)\]. A zero-data reasoning framework that improves
the base model through iterative training data the model generates
itself, without a code executor.

Socratic-Zero \[[22](#bib.bib8)\]. A self-evolving approach that starts
from 100 seed problems. It trains a Solver and a Generator under
guidance from a fixed, high-capacity Teacher, without a Python code
executor.

Agent0 \[[25](#bib.bib6)\]. Agent0 trains a Curriculum Agent to propose
tasks and an Executor Agent to solve them through Python tool use. The
Agent0 baseline retains Ambiguity-Dynamic Policy Optimization (ADPO),
which adjusts advantage weights and clipping bounds according to answer
agreement. AnchorLoop retains both ADPO components and introduces an
iterative anchor into the Executor advantage and the Curriculum reward.

All baselines that involve training use the same Qwen3-4B-Base and
MiMo-7B-Base backbones and the same evaluation protocol as AnchorLoop.
All results in tables were obtained from evaluations conducted in this
work.

SuperGPQA \[[12](#bib.bib17)\]. A question answering benchmark at the
graduate level, spanning over two hundred academic disciplines.

benchmark with broader reasoning across fourteen subject areas.

BBEH \[[7](#bib.bib19)\]. BIG-Bench Extra Hard is a $`23`$-task

counterpart targeting related reasoning skills.

GPQA-Diamond \[[18](#bib.bib22)\]. The most challenging subset of the
GPQA benchmark, designed to be unsolvable through simple retrieval.

HumanEval \[[1](#bib.bib23)\]. A Python code generation benchmark with
handwritten programming problems, each accompanied by unit tests.

AGIEval \[[29](#bib.bib24)\]. A benchmark centered on human examinations
that evaluates foundation models on tasks drawn from standardized tests.

## Appendix D Anchor Mechanism Analysis

This section provides a deeper analysis of the iterative anchor that
underlies AnchorLoop. We quantify the compute and memory overhead it
introduces, compare alternative refresh schedules, measure the
efficiency gain of caching anchor rollouts, and describe the failure
modes where the anchor stops contributing useful signal.

### D.1 Historical-Advantage Structure

We analyze matched records from the first outer iteration for
Qwen3-4B-Base and MiMo-7B-Base. For each backbone, records from each of
five runs are ordered by Executor update step and divided into early,
middle, and late thirds before the stage counts are aggregated. A
candidate matched group is valid when the current and anchor groups
correspond to the same task and Curriculum batch, both records are
complete, and both groups have a resolved majority answer. Invalid
outputs, unresolved ties, and incomplete matches are excluded.

We classify the historical advantage from the discrete reward-indicator
patterns. Its centered vector is zero only when all entries are exactly
zero. A nonzero historical vector is collinear when the current vector
is also nonzero and the two vectors are related by a positive scale.
Negative proportionality and a nonzero historical vector paired with a
zero current vector are classified as non-collinear. Thus, no numerical
tolerance is used. The same-majority rate is reported separately and can
overlap with the zero category.

Table
[6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ D.1 Historical-Advantage Structure ‣ Appendix D Anchor Mechanism Analysis ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
reports the resulting statistics. Each run contributes 120 candidate
groups per stage, giving 600 per stage and backbone. These descriptive
counts characterize the analyzed records but do not establish that the
historical term causes the performance gains in the main results.

|----|----|----|----|----|----|

Table
[9](#A4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ D.4 Anchor Caching Efficiency ‣ Appendix D Anchor Mechanism Analysis ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
compares cached and uncached AnchorLoop on the same eight GPUs and
comparable single-iteration training. The cached version samples $`G=8`$
anchor rollouts once per task and Curriculum batch, then reuses them
across relevant Executor steps. The uncached version resamples $`G=8`$
at each such step. The five-run mean falls from $`32.7`$ to $`24.1`$
hours, a $`26.3\%`$ reduction. Since resampling changes stochastic
outputs, this comparison of complete implementations neither isolates a

overhead.

### D.5 Failure Case Analysis

The iterative anchor stops contributing useful signal in two
identifiable regimes. We describe each with a representative example
taken from our Curriculum logs on Qwen3-4B-Base.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

These cases illustrate two distinct sources of uninformative anchor
feedback. In the first case, the geometry and optimization task yields
dispersed, tied answers, leaving neither sampled group with a unique
modal label. In the second case, both groups count linear arrangements
instead of circular arrangements and overlook rotational equivalence.
Their shared incorrect modal answer makes $`A^{\mathrm{hist}}=0`$, while
$`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ can still compare agreement rates without
identifying the mistake. These examples illustrate that useful anchor
feedback depends on the sampled answer composition and that shared
reasoning errors can remain undetected.

monotonically across iterations under both methods, so the iteration
average gains in Figure
[4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Curriculum frontier fraction. ‣ E.2 Iteration Dynamics on MiMo-7B-Base ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(a)
are not driven by trading off one column against another. Second,
AnchorLoop’s per-step gain is consistently larger than Agent0’s after
iteration $`1`$. The average gap widens from $`0.4`$ at $`t=1`$ to
$`1.4`$ at $`t=2`$ and $`2.5`$ at $`t=3`$, which matches the increasing
separation reported in Figure
[4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Curriculum frontier fraction. ‣ E.2 Iteration Dynamics on MiMo-7B-Base ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(a).
Third, the largest absolute gains over the tool-augmented base appear on
the harder benchmarks. AnchorLoop lifts Minerva by $`9.2`$ points,
AIME25 by $`8.5`$, and AIME24 by $`7.9`$, while the easier GSM8K column
moves by only $`4.6`$ points because it already starts above $`91\%`$.
Agent0 also gains the most on these harder benchmarks, but consistently
by smaller margins, so the AnchorLoop advantage is largest precisely on
the columns with the most headroom.

### E.2 Iteration Dynamics on MiMo-7B-Base

##### Iteration-wise math performance.

Figure
[4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Curriculum frontier fraction. ‣ E.2 Iteration Dynamics on MiMo-7B-Base ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(a)
tracks math AVG on MiMo-7B-Base. Both methods start from the
tool-augmented base at $`56.5`$. Agent0 improves by $`+2.9`$ on
iteration $`1`$, then by only $`+1.1`$ and $`+0.5`$, the same plateau
pattern observed on Qwen3-4B-Base. AnchorLoop improves by $`+3.3`$
points on iteration $`1`$ and continues to gain $`+2.1`$ and $`+1.6`$
points in the next two iterations. The gap to Agent0 therefore widens
from $`0`$ at iteration $`0`$ to $`2.5`$ at iteration $`3`$. The
iteration-$`3`$ endpoints match Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"),
and the same gap of $`2.5`$ points carries over from Qwen3-4B-Base,
indicating that the iterative anchor scales with backbone capability
rather than producing a fixed offset.

##### Effective advantage variance.

Figure
[4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Curriculum frontier fraction. ‣ E.2 Iteration Dynamics on MiMo-7B-Base ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(b)
reports the same stage-averaged within-group variance
$`V_{\mathrm{adv}}`$ defined in Section
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
Agent0 begins at $`0.44`$, while AnchorLoop begins at $`0.45`$. By
iteration $`3`$, Agent0 decreases to $`0.08`$, whereas AnchorLoop
remains at $`0.30`$. These stage averages summarize the sampled Executor
groups and do not imply that the historical term is nonzero in every
group. Under the definitions in Section
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Executor: Cross-Reference Advantage ‣ 3 Method ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents"),
both advantage terms vanish when all current answers in a group are
identical. The observed difference is consistent with greater
within-group variation for AnchorLoop in the evaluated MiMo runs. This
panel alone does not isolate a causal effect on performance.

##### Curriculum frontier fraction.

Figure
[4](#A5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Curriculum frontier fraction. ‣ E.2 Iteration Dynamics on MiMo-7B-Base ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(c)
follows the construction in Figure
[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 4.3 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(c).
Its two groups are sampled independently from the same checkpoint, and
an unresolved pair contributes zero. At iteration $`0`$, the reported
fraction is $`56.2\%`$ for Agent0 and $`56.4\%`$ for AnchorLoop. By
iteration $`3`$, it decreases to $`17.2\%`$ for Agent0 and to $`33.7\%`$
for AnchorLoop. These values record how often independently sampled
groups produce a positive majority agreement gap. They do not measure
correctness, identify newly solved tasks, or establish that the frontier
reward caused the later performance difference. At iteration 3 on both
backbones, AnchorLoop reports higher math AVG, higher effective
advantage variance, and a larger positive agreement gap fraction. These
concurrent differences do not establish a causal relation among the
statistics.

### E.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity on MiMo-7B-Base

![Refer to caption](2610.09856v1/figs/figure_6.png)

Figure 5: Hyperparameter sensitivity on MiMo-7B-Base, the appendix
counterpart of Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Contribution of the two anchor signals. ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(b).
Math AVG on a $`4\times 4`$ grid over the historical-advantage weight
$`\alpha`$ and the frontier reward weight $`\lambda`$. The peak at our
default $`(\alpha,\lambda)=(0.6,0.4)`$ reaches $`63.50`$, matching Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Training Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").

We sweep $`\alpha\in\{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\}`$ and
$`\lambda\in\{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\}`$ on MiMo-7B-Base, the same grid used
for Qwen3-4B-Base in Figure
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Contribution of the two anchor signals. ‣ 4.4 Anchor Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")(b).
Figure
[5](#A5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ E.3 Hyperparameter Sensitivity on MiMo-7B-Base ‣ Appendix E Additional Experimental Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
reports math AVG at each grid cell. The default setting
$`(\alpha,\lambda)=(0.6,0.4)`$ attains the highest reported Math AVG on
both evaluated grids. On MiMo-7B-Base, Math AVG ranges from $`60.47`$ to
$`63.50`$, indicating greater sensitivity than on Qwen3-4B-Base. The
default setting remains the highest-performing point on both evaluated
grids. These results do not establish robustness outside the tested
ranges or prove that the weights transfer across backbones without
selection.

## Appendix F Case Studies and Qualitative Examples

This appendix provides case-level context for the quantitative analyses
in Sections
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Training Dynamics ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
and
[4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 Curriculum Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments and Results ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").
Section
[F.1](#A6.SS1 "F.1 Extended Post-update Executor Comparisons ‣ Appendix F Case Studies and Qualitative Examples ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
compares twelve Curriculum tasks across three outer iterations and
several mathematical topics. Section
[F.2](#A6.SS2 "F.2 Selected Curriculum Tasks Across Outer Iterations ‣ Appendix F Case Studies and Qualitative Examples ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
groups eight topic sequences, each containing one task from iterations
$`0`$ through $`3`$. The grouping organizes related prompts for
comparison and does not establish that a later task was produced by
editing the earlier tasks. Section
[F.3](#A6.SS3 "F.3 Full Executor Reasoning Traces ‣ Appendix F Case Studies and Qualitative Examples ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents")
reports four full reasoning traces, with three AIME 2024 problems and
one Curriculum task from iteration $`3`$. It places selected anchor and
post-update Executor traces side by side. All cases are drawn from runs
on Qwen3-4B-Base.

### F.1 Extended Post-update Executor Comparisons

We report twelve selected Curriculum tasks, with four examples from each
outer iteration $`t\in\{1,2,3\}`$. For each task, we show a displayed
anchor output in gray and a displayed post-update Executor output in

[1](#S2.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Evolve With a Reference:Anchored Training of Tool-Integrated Agents").

by themselves verify the group-level condition
$`\mu^{\mathrm{cur}}(x)>\mu^{\mathrm{anc}}(x)`$, estimate how often the
differences occur, or establish that $`R_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ caused them.

##### Observations in the four selected traces.

Trace 1 displays a batch split in which some anchor rollouts use
$`2.24`$ hours instead of $`2.4`$ for $`2`$h $`24`$m. Trace 2 displays
confusion between counts for exactly $`k`$ groups and pairwise or triple
intersection counts. Trace 3 displays an error in positional value,
where the anchor treats $`\overline{ad}`$ as $`a+d`$ rather than
$`10a+d`$. Trace 4 displays an incomplete search that stops at the first
positive hit. The displayed post-update Executor traces use Python
checks before reporting their final answers. These cases show how Python
is used in the selected solutions, but they do not establish that Python
caused robustness or that the pattern holds across tasks.
